b: The Open Measurement SDK (OM SDK) is a piece of shared software, maintained by the IAB Tech Lab, that publishers and ad platforms build into mobile apps, web video players and connected TV (CTV) devices so that independent measurement companies can check whether an ad was on screen, for how long and on what kind of device. It exists because apps, unlike web pages, do not let an outside tag look around freely. Before it arrived, each verification vendor wanted its own software development kit (SDK) inside every app. OM SDK replaces that stack with one integration that any certified vendor can read.

The system has three parts. The first is the SDK itself, which a publisher or an ad network compiles into its own app or ad SDK. The second is the Open Measurement Interface Definition (OMID), the application programming interface (API) through which the SDK exposes what it observes. The third is the verification script, a small piece of JavaScript supplied by a measurement vendor such as Integral Ad Science (IAS), DoubleVerify or Comscore, which runs alongside the ad and listens to OMID.

A typical in-app impression follows a fixed sequence. The integrating SDK starts an ad session when an ad is about to render. It loads each vendor's verification script, passes along any vendor-specific parameters, and then reports a stream of events: that the ad loaded, that it began to render, how large the ad view is, what share of it is visible, and whether anything is covering it. For video it adds playback milestones such as start and quartiles, plus volume and player state. The vendor's script turns those raw signals into its own judgement about viewability or invalid activity and reports back to the vendor's servers. The SDK itself does not decide whether an impression is viewable.

Identity matters in that pipe. Each certified integration carries an OMID partner name and version string, and those travel into the auction. In OpenRTB, according to the IAB Tech Lab's 2018 working draft on OM SDK support, a seller signals that a placement can be measured by including the value 7 ("OMID-1") in the api array of a banner, video or native object, and passes the partner name and version as omidpn and omidpv in source.ext. Native ads declare verification through an event tracker with event type 555 and the JavaScript method. In video, the scripts arrive inside the AdVerifications node that VAST 4.1 made standard, or through an extension in VAST 2 and 3.

Two details shape the numbers buyers see. Friendly obstructions let a publisher flag elements that legitimately sit on top of an ad, such as video player controls, so vendors do not mark the ad as hidden. Misuse would hide genuine obstructions, one reason certification exists. IAB Tech Lab certifies each integration and publishes the list of compliant partners through a compliance API.

On the buy side, platforms set their own rules for who can run code. Google's Authorized Buyers help page, for example, accepts OM verification on app video, display and rewarded formats across open auction, private auction, preferred deals and Programmatic Guaranteed, lists 17 approved vendor domains, and disapproves creatives that use OMID scripts outside the public API (code 721) or call a vendor that is not on the list (code 752).

The project began with a donation. IAS handed code to the IAB Tech Lab in 2017, according to an AdExchanger opinion piece by Joseph Ranzenbach of IAS, and the founding vendors, IAS, Moat, DoubleVerify, Comscore and Nielsen, agreed not to push their own legacy SDKs. General availability followed in April 2018.

By December 2019 more than 50 integrations had been certified, including Google, Pandora, Hulu, InMobi, Gameloft, NBCUniversal, TikTok and Teads, according to AdExchanger. IAS told the publication its share of in-app impressions measured through Open Measurement rose from about 1% in September 2018 to roughly 60% a year later. In August 2019 Google said it would enable Open Measurement on more than 85% of in-app display and video impressions from AdMob and Ad Manager publishers.

Version 1.3 of OMID, released on December 17, 2019, was a minor, backward-compatible release that added audio as a media type, content URLs for in-app brand safety checks, and new "ad loaded" and "begin to render" events meant to close impression count gaps. A separate OM Web Video SDK followed in December 2020; it is not backward compatible with the older web SDK.

CTV came next. On June 8, 2022, the IAB Tech Lab said OM SDK would reach tvOS and Android TV from the third quarter of that year, with signals specific to television such as whether the set is switched off and when the viewer last interacted. OMID 1.4 added those CTV events. In May 2022 Google said Active View, its viewability system in Ad Manager, would switch from a proprietary method to Open Measurement for mobile app display inventory, without giving a date.

On May 30, 2024, OM SDK 1.5 extended CTV support to Samsung and LG televisions through the web video SDK. The IAB Tech Lab claimed this brought coverage to about 40% of CTVs in households. On June 11, 2025, version 1.5.5 began passing the UniversalAdId from VAST into each ad session, so vendors can tie a measurement to a specific creative registered with a body such as Ad-ID. As of November 2026 the current API documentation is OMID 1.6.

For buyers, OM SDK is what makes in-app and CTV viewability comparable across sellers. Without it, a viewability rate in one app came from one vendor's SDK and a rate in the next app from another, or from the publisher's own counting. With it, the same verification script runs everywhere a certified integration exists. That consistency feeds accreditation: the Media Rating Council audits the vendors that read OM signals, and recent decisions, such as DoubleVerify's CTV viewability accreditation in April 2024 and HUMAN Security's display and video accreditation, cover app environments where OM is the usual signal source.

It also underpins changes in how impressions are counted and billed. Viewability depends on knowing when an ad actually rendered, and the industry's move to begin-to-render counting relies on render events of the kind OMID 1.3 introduced. Google drops unrendered ads from DV360 and CM360 billing in February 2027, and Amazon expects about 63% fewer display impressions once only on-screen ads count from January 1, 2027. Neither change is an OM SDK release, but both reward environments that can prove an ad was seen.

The oldest criticism is about demand. Ranzenbach wrote in December 2019 that it was "not time for a victory lap yet", because buyers on the open exchange could not target OM-enabled inventory and very few demand-side platforms (DSPs) used the OpenRTB signals. Google's own 2019 announcement carried a plea from Dennis Buchheim, then at the IAB Tech Lab, for brands, agencies and DSPs to "get more active".

Coverage remains partial. The 40% CTV figure is the IAB Tech Lab's own claim and leaves most television screens outside the standard, and Google's Authorized Buyers documentation limits CTV support to inventory served through its Interactive Media Ads (IMA) SDK. Trust is another issue: the SDK runs inside the publisher's or ad network's code, so its signals are only as honest as the integration, which is why certification and device checks keep being added. The IAB Tech Lab's Device Attestation work adapts the Internet Engineering Task Force's Privacy Pass protocol so measurement partners can confirm an impression rendered on a genuine device.

Performance has been a cost too. Verification scripts traditionally run in a WebView, which is heavy on low-end Android phones. An October 2026 IAB Tech Lab post reported that running scripts in Android's JavaScriptEngine sandbox cut first session creation from 268 ms to about 11 ms on one unnamed low-end device, a benchmark of ten cold starts rather than a field study.
OMID is the interface, not the software. OM SDK implements OMID; vendors write scripts against OMID.
MRAID (Mobile Rich Media Ad Interface Definitions) governs how rich media creatives talk to an app, for example to expand or close. It is about ad behaviour, while OM SDK is about measurement.

VPAID (Video Player-Ad Interface Definition) once carried measurement code inside video ads. Google says it never accepted VPAID on app inventory, and OM SDK, with VAST AdVerifications, removed the need for it.
Mobile measurement partners, covered in PPC Land's explainer, attribute installs and in-app events to campaigns. They answer "which ad drove this install", not "was this ad seen".

In October 2026 the IAB Tech Lab described how OM SDK for Android 1.6.10 lets native ad sessions run verification scripts in the JavaScriptEngine sandbox, an opt-in path that cut Android ad session start to 11 ms in its test, with HTML and JavaScript sessions not yet supported. In November 2026 the IAB Tech Lab extended OM SDK support to the formats in its CTV Ad Portfolio: Pause, Menu or Homescreen, Screensaver and Overlay ads. "CTV advertising is moving fast, and measurement has to move with it," said Jill Wittkopp, vice president of product at the IAB Tech Lab, according to MediaNews4U. Whether buyers will price those formats on OM-based measurement, as they gradually did with app video, is the open question.

Who: The IAB Tech Lab maintains OM SDK. Publishers, ad networks and streaming platforms integrate it; verification vendors such as IAS, DoubleVerify and Comscore write scripts that read it; buyers and platforms such as Google decide which vendors may run.

What: A shared SDK and interface (OMID) that collects viewability and related signals inside apps, web video players and CTV devices and hands them to independent measurement scripts, replacing a separate SDK for each vendor.
When: General availability in April 2018, audio and render events in December 2019, web video in December 2020, CTV from 2022, Samsung and LG in May 2024, and new CTV formats in November 2026.
Where: iOS and Android apps, web video players, and CTV platforms including tvOS, Android TV, Samsung and LG, with signals passed into OpenRTB bid requests and VAST responses.

Why: Apps and televisions block the outside tags that measure web display ads, so the industry needed one certified, neutral way to let independent vendors verify that ads were seen, without loading every app with competing code.
